newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's new parliament opens without Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's new parliament opens without Serbs.

text.p: Moslem and Croat legislators opened Bosnia's new inter-ethnic parliament on Saturday, ignoring a boycott by Serbs who refused to swear an oath to Bosnian statehood.

International mediators failed to broker a compromise that would satisfy hardline nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of the elected three-man presidency, and the 10 Serb members of the parliament.

After delaying the ceremony for several hours, Croat and Moslem deputies held the first session without the Serbs. As foreign dignitaries looked on at Sarajevo's national theatre, they signed an oath of loyalty to the Bosnian constitution.
Krajisnik and the 10 Serbs refused to sign because the oath obliges members to swear loyalty to Bosnia as a unitary state, a concept which they have bitterly opposed.

"I commit myself to support and defend the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina," the oath read in part. It also called for defending the equality of national communities and "to fully respect the peace agreement."

Croat and Moslem deputies decided to hold the session to show solidarity and support for the peace process, said Duncan Bullitvant, a spokesman for the international High Representive to Bosnia, Carl Bildt.
He described the Serb stance as "puerile and ridiculous, but, in the absence of the Serbs, the legal weight of the session remained unclear.
Although Moslem and Croat deputies signed an oath of office, Bullivant said the proceedings could not be considered an inauguration without the Serbs.

The three-member presidency, which has met once, had also been due to be inaugurated on Saturday. Bildt's office said the body already had legal powers and the proceedings had been meant purely as a "ceremoninal" ratification.
Two members of the presidency, the Moslem chairman, Alija Izetbegovic, and Kresimir Zubak, a Croat, sat on the theatre stage next to an empty chair reserved for Krajisnik.
After they signed the oath, Izetbegovic delivered what he said was the speech he had prepared assuming the Serbs would show up.
Addressing the absent Serbs, he said: "Feel safe, this is your town too, because Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina."
Michael Steiner, a deputy to Bildt, emerged empty-handed from three hours of talks with Krajisnik at the Serb government seat of Pale, 16 km (10 miles) outside Sarajevo.
Krajisnik had warned on Friday that the Serbs were not satisfied with the venue and the oath for the parliamentary meeting.
The 42-member House of Representatives and the three-man collective presidency were elected on September 14, nine months after the Dayton peace accord was signed.
